transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I keep getting stuck on how sagging and uneven my jaw and one side of my face look. It really hit me after seeing the family photos. My wife and even my clients say they barely notice anything, but I see it pretty clearly.

When your wife or clients tell you they don't notice any unevenness, do you think it's possible they're right and you might be misjudging it, or are you completely certain that what you see is real no matter what they say?
I mean, I hear what they’re saying, but when I look at the photos I still see the sagging around my jaw and the unevenness on that side of my face. It’s hard for me to believe I’m just imagining it.

If you had to put a number on it, how convinced are you that your jaw and face are actually uneven—are you 100% certain this is true, or is there still some part of you that thinks you might be wrong?

I’m pretty convinced when I see the photos—maybe not 100%, because my wife keeps telling me she doesn’t see it. But it still looks like there’s sagging around my jaw and that one side is uneven to me.

Aside from concerns about your jaw and face, have you noticed any other unusual beliefs or experiences lately, such as feeling that people are watching you, talking about you, or that something else out of the ordinary is happening?
No, I haven’t noticed anything like that. I don’t feel like people are watching me or talking about me.
Do you find yourself frequently checking mirrors, comparing your face to old photos, or trying to camouflage or fix the way your jaw looks—like with makeup, angles, or facial hair?

Yeah. Before client meetings, I’ll check the bathroom mirror and my phone camera several times. I mess with the lighting, change my collar, or turn my face a certain way. And I catch myself comparing my face to younger advisors or people at gallery events instead of really paying attention to the conversation.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports persistent preoccupation with a perceived defect (facial/jaw asymmetry) that is not observable or appears only slight to others, causing significant distress and repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, camera checking, camouflaging with collar/lighting/angles) and comparison with others (younger advisors, gallery attendees), consistent with Body Dysmorphic Disorder. Insight is poor but not absent—patient acknowledges some uncertainty ('maybe not 100%') when confronted with feedback from wife and clients, ruling out a delusional disorder (F22) where conviction would be fixed and unshakeable. No other psychotic symptoms (paranoia, ideas of reference) were endorsed, further supporting BDD with poor insight rather than a primary psychotic disorder.
